extracted.intended_audience: general public, journalists, researchers and fact-checkers interested in COVID-19 misinformation
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic summary cataloguing false or misleading claims about COVID-19, with factual corrections, evidence summaries, platform moderation actions, and instances of harms resulting from misinformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 5G and COVID-19 causation claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The first conspiracy theories purporting a link between COVID-19 and 5G mobile networks had already appeared by the end of January 2020; claims that 5G caused COVID-19 are false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes examples (Thomas Cowan, Mark Steele, Kate Shemirani), harms (arson attacks on masts, threats to engineers), and platform responses (YouTube reduced recommendation/removed videos linking 5G and COVID-19). Also emphasizes scientific rebuttal: viruses cannot be transmitted by radio waves and COVID-19 has spread in many countries without 5G.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform moderation policy for conspiratorial 5G content
rubrics_metrics.description: YouTube announced that it would reduce the amount of content claiming links between 5G and COVID-19; videos that are conspiratorial about 5G that do not mention COVID-19 would not be removed but might be considered 'borderline content' and removed from search recommendations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains enforcement nuance: direct COVID-19-5G claims targeted for suppression/removal, derivative 5G conspiracies may lose monetization or recommendation but not necessarily be removed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadcasting standards re: potentially harmful claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Ofcom found an interview expressing views 'which had the potential to cause significant harm to viewers' and said comments were 'ambiguous' and 'ill-judged' and 'risked undermining viewers' trust in advice from public authorities and scientific evidence'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as an example of regulator action against media that propagate or lend credibility to misinformation which may harm public health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific fact: viruses and radio waves
rubrics_metrics.description: Viruses cannot be transmitted by radio waves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to rebut 5G-related transmission theories; contextualized with evidence that COVID-19 spread in locations without 5G and expert statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: RT-PCR sensitivity and interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: The reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) test for SARS-CoV-2 is highly sensitive to the virus, and testing laboratories have controls in place to prevent and detect contamination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies common misinterpretations: PCR detects presence of viral RNA but does not by itself indicate whether the virus is infectious; some viral critics misrepresented Kary Mullis' comments. Laboratories use controls to reduce false positives/contamination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of PCR tests (infectiousness vs detection)
rubrics_metrics.description: The tests only reveal the presence of the virus and not whether it remains infectious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why some criticisms that PCR 'cannot detect infectious virus' are misunderstandings of what the test measures; this distinction is important when evaluating claims about test reliability and policy inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surface/fomite transmission risk assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) concluded that the likelihood of transmission under these scenarios was less than 1 in 10,000 and that handwashing reduced the risk of exposure to COVID-19, but surface disinfection did not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to correct early misinformation that fomites were a major route; informs recommended prevention: prioritize handwashing over excessive surface disinfection for typical situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hand hygiene guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Washing in soap and water for at least 20 seconds is the best way to clean hands. The second-best is a hand sanitizer that is at least 60% alcohol.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains common misinformation that sanitizers are 'antibacterial not antiviral' is misleading; most commercial hand sanitizers inactivate SARS-CoV-2. CDC/FDA recommend plain soap; antibacterial soaps offer no proven advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Face mask guidance and changing advice over time
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorities recommended mask use in many places early on (especially in Asia); other parts of the world initially dismissed masks with misleading or incomplete information about their effectiveness. Additional scientific evidence resulted in different advice over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames anti-mask messaging sometimes as rationing/shortage management or outright misinformation; indicates that evolving evidence changed guidance and that contrary early statements were sometimes misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excess deaths as a measure of COVID-19 mortality
rubrics_metrics.description: The CDC collects data based on case surveillance, vital records, and excess deaths; in the U.S. there were 882,000 'excess deaths' between February 2020 and January 2022 which is somewhat higher than officially recorded COVID-19 mortality (835,000) and strongly correlated with infections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to refute claims that deaths were vastly overcounted; explains appropriate data sources and why excess deaths are a robust cross-check against misclassification or reporting issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for extraordinary origin claims (e.g., meteor origin)
rubrics_metrics.description: A group speculated COVID-19 originated from a meteor but 'did not provide any direct evidence proving this conjecture.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrates the standard that extraordinary causal claims require direct evidence; absence of direct evidence means the claim remains speculative and should not be presented as established fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for reporting case counts and transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Correctly reporting the number of people who were sick or who had died was difficult; leaked documents indicated official reporting gave an incomplete picture (example: China reporting fewer confirmed cases than internal documents showed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Points to the need for multiple data streams (confirmed, clinically diagnosed, suspected), transparency, and careful interpretation of official tallies when evaluating claims about under- or over-reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation of claims about population susceptibility by ethnicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that specific ethnicities are more or less vulnerable to COVID-19 are unsupported; COVID-19 is a new zoonotic disease so no population had prior population immunity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example rebuttals: far-right or xenophobic claims were debunked; scientific consensus does not support race-based innate immunity claims. Cautions against policy or social conclusions based on unverified genetic susceptibility assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence incorporation and WHO position on airborne spread
rubrics_metrics.description: Before mid-2021 the World Health Organization (WHO) denied that COVID readily spread through the air; later, hundreds of scientists called on WHO to change its position and evidence was incorporated indicating airborne spread can occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to show how authoritative guidance can lag evolving scientific consensus and why claims that earlier WHO positions prove absence of airborne spread are misleading; emphasizes the need to follow updated guidance as evidence accrues.
